what_it_does: A Bayesian neural network (BNN) is a kind of AI model that, instead of giving a single confident answer, outputs a range of possibilities — which is important in safety-critical applications like robot perception where overconfidence can be dangerous. The problem is that generating the required randomness in software is very expensive and too slow for real-time use on small robots. This paper builds a mixed-signal (part digital, part analog) hardware chip that exploits a quantum physics phenomenon called tunneling — where electrons occasionally leak through a barrier they classically should not cross — inside a special type of transistor (a fully depleted silicon-on-insulator, or FDSOI, transistor) to produce statistically well-behaved random numbers at very low energy (200 femtojoules per sample, which is extremely cheap). These random numbers feed a parallel BNN hardware engine that runs probabilistic inference at low latency. The approach is claimed to dramatically reduce the hardware cost of uncertainty-aware AI compared to conventional software BNNs, though the full evaluation details are not available from the abstract alone.
